newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Lotus deal gives Proton technology control.
newsitem.headline: Lotus deal gives Proton technology control.

text.p: Malaysian car maker Proton is gaining control of technology it needs to expand its business through the 80 percent purchase of British sports car maker Group Lotus Ltd, auto analysts said on Thursday.

After a week of speculation, Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd (Proton) and its chairman Yahaya Ahmad confirmed on Wednesday that they jointly bought the Lotus controlling stake for 51 million stg ($82.88 million).
Foreign tie-ups are common for Proton, maker of a ubiquitous Malaysian car modelled on Japanese autos. Its models include the Proton Saga, Iswara, Wira, Tiara and Perdana.

Proton has had a decade-long agreement with Japan's Mitsubishi for the supply of car parts like engines. Earlier this year, Proton announced a collaboration with Automobiles Citroen of France for a model called Tiara based on the Citroen AX Model.
But the pact with Lotus, which provides design engineering services and technology, goes beyond just a partnership to ownership, analysts noted.

"The reason to take up the 80 percent stake is to speed up the technology transfer," said one equities dealer with a local brokerage firm. "You actually own the company. With Citroen and Mitsubishi, it was a technology link-up."
Lotus makes luxury sports cars including the Lotus Seven, the Lotus Elan, the Elite and the new model, the Elise.
As part of the deal, Proton will start producing Elise cars in Malaysia. Yahaya said the company will make about 2,500 Elise cars a year in Malaysia.
"In the long-term, Proton may want to aim for its own engine," said Goh Keat Jin, an auto analyst at PhileoAllied Securities. "Lotus has a good track record on that."
Proton has set a goal of producing 500,000 cars by the end of the decade. It made 160,000 cars in 1995.
Analysts said the Lotus stake could help Malaysia reduce its dependency on Japanese-made car parts, which contribute to the country's balance of payments problem.

The move to higher technology could also become important as Malaysia's automobile market faces more competition with Asia moving towards free trade, said Audrey Ho, head of research at Mohaiyani Securities.
"In order to upgrade the image of the car, they want something slightly different," Ho said. "They are eyeing a greater market niche and they want a cutting edge."

Investors seemed to welcome the Lotus deal, bidding up Proton's stock 2.5 percent in early trading on Thursday to 16.20 ringgit ($6.48). Near the end of the session, the stock had cut its gains to 16.00 ringgit, up 20 cents.
But analysts said they do not expect Proton to reap any quick economic benefits from the deal.

"The general market reaction is quite positive," said Ami Moris, a vice president in equities dealing at Capitalcorp. "But I don't think it's going to impact earnings immediately. It may, sometime way in the future."
